To be completely honest: **No, you will not be able to see the Moon with your naked eyes under these conditions.**

Here is the breakdown of why, based on the data you provided:

### 1. The "Daylight" Problem
The most significant factor is the **Sun's altitude (43.368 degrees)**. At this angle, the Sun is high enough in the sky to scatter a massive amount of sunlight through the atmosphere. This creates "bright daylight" conditions. 

In astronomy, the Moon is only visible during the day if it is very close to the Sun (a thin crescent) or if it is a Full Moon near the horizon at twilight. Because your Moon is **58% illuminated** (a Waxing Gibbous), it is far enough from the Sun to be "fuller," but it is still being completely washed out by the overwhelming brightness of the daytime sky.

### 2. The Contrast Gap
Your eyes work on contrast. During the day, the atmosphere is saturated with scattered blue light. For an object to be visible to the unaided eye, it must be significantly brighter than the surrounding sky. Even though the Moon is a large object, it does not have enough "luminance" to compete with the brightness of a 43-degree Sun. It will be there, but it will be invisible to your eyes.

### 3. The Geometry
*   **The Sun** is at an azimuth of **85.6°** (roughly East).
*   **The Moon** is at an azimuth of **232.2°** (roughly Southwest).

While the Moon is in a different part of the sky than the Sun, the "glare" of the day covers the entire dome of the sky. It’s like trying to see a flashlight beam pointed at you while someone is shining a massive stadium floodlight into the atmosphere nearby—the ambient light simply drowns out the smaller source.

### The Verdict
If you were to look toward the Southwest (Azimuth 232°), you would see a bright, clear blue sky. You would not see the Moon.

**When could you see it?**
To see this specific Moon, you would need to wait until the Sun sets. Since the Moon is 99 degrees away from the Sun, it will remain above the horizon for several hours after the Sun goes down. Once the "blue" of the day fades into the "black" of night, the Moon will pop out brilliantly!
